data.claim: No: _toml_literal (json.dumps, ensure_ascii=True) is not a correct TOML string writer for arbitrary text: it leaves values like 'true' or '[x]' unquoted, and writes non-BMP chars as surrogate pairs TOML refuses; json.dumps(ensure_ascii=False) plus escaping U+007F round-trips every string.

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff replaces `_TOLERANT_VALUES = frozenset({"mcp.tools", "export.refresh", "export.tables"})` with `frozenset({*KNOB_CHOICES, "export.tables"})`, i.e. it makes *every* newly-validated enum knob tolerant. Per the surviving code comment, a tolerant knob's value in a config FILE "is skipped with a warning rather than refused". So the file-load path reintroduces exactly the failure this bug is about: with a config file containing

    [enforce]
    stale_docs = "blok"

the value is no longer refused (a check now exists, but it is bypassed for tolerant knobs); it is skipped with a warning and the knob falls back to its default, i.e. the misspelt policy still "quietly behaves as some other value". The fix only refuses on the write path (`Config.check` / `config set`), which is the exact probe in the report, so a test that only calls `Config.check` will pass while the actual file-driven behavior remains. It is also a concrete behavioral regression for at least `dedupe.on_match`, which the intent states was previously refused on load (`_KNOB_CHECKS`-checked and *not* tolerant); after this change it is in `KNOB_CHOICES`, therefore in `_TOLERANT_VALUES`, so an invalid `dedupe.on_match` in a config file is downgraded from a hard refusal to a warning-plus-default. The original comment scoped tolerance to knobs "whose VALUE set can grow in a later release"; fixed domains such as `enforce.*` (`block | warn | off`) and `dedupe.on_match` do not qualify, so blanket tolerance defeats the stated guarantee.

chunk_findings.detail: In a dict display, later keys overwrite earlier ones, so putting the derived block last means every knob that appears both in `KNOB_CHOICES` and in the hand-written table loses its hand-written validator. The entry immediately above the spread, `dedupe.kinds`, is exactly one of the enum knobs this change is meant to cover: its allowed values are the enumerated `DEDUPE_KINDS`, so it is a natural member of `KNOB_CHOICES`. Its hand-written check is list-aware (`isinstance(v, list) and all(x in DEDUPE_KINDS for x in v)`), but once the spread is expanded after it, `_one_of(DEDUPE_KINDS)` takes precedence and performs scalar membership. A valid config such as `dedupe.kinds = ["plan"]` is then tested as `["plan"] in DEDUPE_KINDS`, which is `False`, so a legal value is reported as "must be one of ..." and refused; the list branch becomes dead code. The regression test described in the intent only asserts that *bad* values are refused, so it will not catch this — it happily passes while valid list-valued knobs are rejected. The derived block needs to be expanded before the hand-written entries (or overlapping keys excluded), otherwise any future/present overlap silently downgrades a specialized validator to a scalar one.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_alternatives` strips every parenthesised group out of the text *before* looking for the `a | b | c` run:

```python
m = re.search(_ALTS, re.sub(r"\s*\([^)]*\)", "", text))
```

so a knob whose allowed values are themselves written as a parenthesised enumeration is silently dropped. Concretely, `_alternatives("(block | warn | off)")` returns `None` (the `re.sub` deletes the whole string, then `re.search` finds nothing), even though the text plainly contains the `block | warn | off` run the function claims to return; `_alternatives("(block | warn) also off | auto")` returns `("off", "auto")`, silently losing `block` and `warn`. Any knob documented as `# (block | warn | off)` is therefore absent from `LISTED`, which means `test_a_value_outside_the_listed_alternatives_is_refused` is never parametrised for it and `Config.check` is never exercised with a bad value for that knob. If the fix forgets/mis-declares the choices for such a knob, this regression suite still passes: the only guard is `test_the_scan_finds_the_knobs_the_bug_named`, which hard-codes six key names and `len(LISTED) >= 21`, so a parser miss can be masked by other knobs. The same hole exists for alternatives written in quotes (`"a" | "b"`, which `_ALTS` cannot match because `"` is not in `[\w-]`) or separated by commas (`a, b, c`); these are exactly the “knob whose allowed values are only written in a comment” cases the change is supposed to catch, and the test docstring’s claim that such a knob “fails here too” holds only when the comment happens to use a bare, unquoted, unparenthesised `a | b | c`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The diff replaces `_TOLERANT_VALUES = frozenset({"mcp.tools", "export.refresh", "export.tables"})` with `frozenset({*KNOB_CHOICES, "export.tables"})`, i.e. it makes *every* newly-validated enum knob tolerant. Per the surviving code comment, a tolerant knob's value in a config FILE "is skipped with a warning rather than refused". So the file-load path reintroduces exactly the failure this bug is about: with a config file containing

    [enforce]
    stale_docs = "blok"

the value is no longer refused (a check now exists, but it is bypassed for tolerant knobs); it is skipped with a warning and the knob falls back to its default, i.e. the misspelt policy still "quietly behaves as some other value". The fix only refuses on the write path (`Config.check` / `config set`), which is the exact probe in the report, so a test that only calls `Config.check` will pass while the actual file-driven behavior remains. It is also a concrete behavioral regression for at least `dedupe.on_match`, which the intent states was previously refused on load (`_KNOB_CHECKS`-checked and *not* tolerant); after this change it is in `KNOB_CHOICES`, therefore in `_TOLERANT_VALUES`, so an invalid `dedupe.on_match` in a config file is downgraded from a hard refusal to a warning-plus-default. The original comment scoped tolerance to knobs "whose VALUE set can grow in a later release"; fixed domains such as `enforce.*` (`block | warn | off`) and `dedupe.on_match` do not qualify, so blanket tolerance defeats the stated guarantee.

chunk_findings.detail: In a dict display, later keys overwrite earlier ones, so putting the derived block last means every knob that appears both in `KNOB_CHOICES` and in the hand-written table loses its hand-written validator. The entry immediately above the spread, `dedupe.kinds`, is exactly one of the enum knobs this change is meant to cover: its allowed values are the enumerated `DEDUPE_KINDS`, so it is a natural member of `KNOB_CHOICES`. Its hand-written check is list-aware (`isinstance(v, list) and all(x in DEDUPE_KINDS for x in v)`), but once the spread is expanded after it, `_one_of(DEDUPE_KINDS)` takes precedence and performs scalar membership. A valid config such as `dedupe.kinds = ["plan"]` is then tested as `["plan"] in DEDUPE_KINDS`, which is `False`, so a legal value is reported as "must be one of ..." and refused; the list branch becomes dead code. The regression test described in the intent only asserts that *bad* values are refused, so it will not catch this — it happily passes while valid list-valued knobs are rejected. The derived block needs to be expanded before the hand-written entries (or overlapping keys excluded), otherwise any future/present overlap silently downgrades a specialized validator to a scalar one.

chunk_findings.detail: The final assertion in the rewritten test is `assert A.check_after_merge(repo, sha=sha).get("status") != "unavailable"`. Using `.get(...)` makes the test pass whenever the key is absent, and the `!= "unavailable"` form passes for any other value, so the test no longer pins down that the merge actually proceeds with the default `fast` mode after an unknown enum value. Concrete failure: if `check_after_merge` regresses to return `{}` (or `{"status": "error", ...}`) for a config whose `ci.on_merge` value was `"sometimes"`, `.get("status")` yields `None` (or `"error"`), which is `!= "unavailable"`, so this test still passes even though the merge did not run as intended. The test is supposed to prove the unknown knob falls back to the default and the merge proceeds, so it should assert the concrete success status/payload (e.g. the same status a valid `on_merge = "fast"` produces) rather than a negation. chunk_findings.detail:
`_alternatives` strips every parenthesised group out of the text *before* looking for the `a | b | c` run:

```python
m = re.search(_ALTS, re.sub(r"\s*\([^)]*\)", "", text))
```

so a knob whose allowed values are themselves written as a parenthesised enumeration is silently dropped. Concretely, `_alternatives("(block | warn | off)")` returns `None` (the `re.sub` deletes the whole string, then `re.search` finds nothing), even though the text plainly contains the `block | warn | off` run the function claims to return; `_alternatives("(block | warn) also off | auto")` returns `("off", "auto")`, silently losing `block` and `warn`. Any knob documented as `# (block | warn | off)` is therefore absent from `LISTED`, which means `test_a_value_outside_the_listed_alternatives_is_refused` is never parametrised for it and `Config.check` is never exercised with a bad value for that knob. If the fix forgets/mis-declares the choices for such a knob, this regression suite still passes: the only guard is `test_the_scan_finds_the_knobs_the_bug_named`, which hard-codes six key names and `len(LISTED) >= 21`, so a parser miss can be masked by other knobs. The same hole exists for alternatives written in quotes (`"a" | "b"`, which `_ALTS` cannot match because `"` is not in `[\w-]`) or separated by commas (`a, b, c`); these are exactly the “knob whose allowed values are only written in a comment” cases the change is supposed to catch, and the test docstring’s claim that such a knob “fails here too” holds only when the comment happens to use a bare, unquoted, unparenthesised `a | b | c`.

chunk_findings.detail: The derived `_one_of(KNOB_CHOICES[key])` predicates were moved from the end of the `_KNOB_CHECKS` literal to the front. In a Python dict literal duplicate keys are not an error — the last occurrence wins — so for any dotted key that is both declared in `KNOB_CHOICES` and given a bespoke entry below, the bespoke predicate now completely shadows the declared-choices predicate and `KNOB_CHOICES` stops being enforced for that key. The inserted comment confirms such overlaps exist ("a hand-written check below for the same key"), and `_KNOB_CHECKS` already contains a bespoke check of this shape, the `dedupe.on_match` predicate, whose message is *"must be a non-empty list drawn from …; to stop the check set [dedupe].on_match = "off""*. Concretely, if `KNOB_CHOICES["dedupe.on_match"]` declares the string choices (e.g. `("off", "error", "warn")`), then before the change `Config.check({"dedupe": {"on_match": "error"}})` passed the derived `_one_of` check (a declared choice), whereas after the reorder the bespoke list check wins and the same input is rejected as "must be a non-empty list …", i.e. the declared choices and the values that are actually accepted now diverge; symmetrically, a value the bespoke predicate tolerates but the choices tuple does not will be accepted. Either way the enum validation the fix was supposed to guarantee for that knob is no longer performed by the declared table.

chunk_findings.detail: This change is a semantics-preserving refactor, so it does not fix the reported bug. The old body built one dict literal as `{**{key: _one_of(allowed) for key, allowed in KNOB_CHOICES.items()}, <hand-written entries>}`; the new code builds `_VALUE_CHECKS` with the exact same hand-written entries and then `_KNOB_CHECKS = {**{derived}, **_VALUE_CHECKS}`. Because Python picks the winner of a duplicate key by position in the literal, and `_VALUE_CHECKS` is still spread *after* the derived comprehension (just as the hand-written entries were before), the resulting mapping has exactly the same keys and values as the old one. Nothing was added to `KNOB_CHOICES` and no hand-written entry was removed. Concretely, `Config.check({'enforce': {'stale_docs': 'blok'}})` and `Config.check({'lease': {'reclaim_policy': 'autoo'}})` still find no check for those keys (they are neither in `KNOB_CHOICES` nor in `_VALUE_CHECKS`) and return `None`, the exact behaviour the bug reports. The intended fix — "declare choices on every enum knob" — requires adding the missing entries to `KNOB_CHOICES` (or parsing the `# block | warn | off` comments); that is absent from the diff, so the enumerated knobs remain unvalidated.

chunk_findings.detail: `kill_group`'s docstring justifies the raw `os.killpg(p.pid, ...)` on the grounds that it is "call[ed] before `p` is reaped, while that pid -- and so the group id -- is still reserved and cannot name a recycled process", but `run_shell` violates that premise on its `except BaseException` path. `Popen.communicate()` (and `Popen.wait()`, bpo-25942) installs its own `KeyboardInterrupt` handler that calls `self._wait(timeout=min(self._sigint_wait_secs, remaining))` -- reaping the child and setting `returncode` -- *before* re-raising the `KeyboardInterrupt`; `Popen.kill()` is safe against this because `send_signal()` calls `self.poll()` first, but `os.killpg` is a raw syscall with no such guard. Concretely: a gate/CI sends SIGINT to the ddflow process while `run_shell(cmd, timeout=None, on_tick=..., tick_s=...)` is inside `p.communicate(timeout=wait)` and `cmd` happens to exit within that ~0.25 s window; `communicate` reaps it, `run_shell` then enters `except BaseException` and calls `kill_group(p)`, and `os.killpg(p.pid, SIGKILL)` addresses a pid that is no longer reserved. If the kernel has since handed that pid to a new process-group leader (e.g. another command started with `start_new_session=True`), the unrelated group is SIGKILLed -- the exact orphan-killing/side-effect failure this change was written to prevent -- and, less severely, the reaped group is empty so the call can only ever return ESRCH here.

chunk_findings.detail:
The previous call pinned the child's stdin to `subprocess.DEVNULL`:

```python
p = P.run(cmd, shell=True, cwd=tree, capture_output=True, text=True,
          timeout=cfg.ci.timeout_s, stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, check=False)
```

The replacement call drops `stdin` entirely. Nothing in this hunk (nor in the visible `P.run_shell` call in `gates.py`, which also omits it) restores it, so if `P.run_shell` follows `subprocess.run`'s default (`stdin=None`, i.e. inherited), the operator's `[ci].command` now reads from the daemon's stdin instead of getting immediate EOF. Concretely: a `[ci].command` such as `git commit` (no `-m`), `read -r …`, or `gh pr merge` without `--yes` previously saw EOF/dev-null and exited immediately; now it can block on the inherited terminal/pipe until `cfg.ci.timeout_s` elapses, at which point the whole process group is killed and `check_merge` reports `"unavailable"` with a timeout reason instead of a successful merge. `P.run_shell` is not shown in this part, so the old `stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL` guarantee is silently lost here.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new probe that is supposed to locate the shell spawn in `ddflow/infra/proc.py` is

```python
call = next(ln for ln in src.splitlines() if "shell=True" in ln and "popen(" in ln)
```

The `"popen("` substring is lowercase and case‑sensitive. The moved shell spawn is `proc.run_shell`, whose body necessarily calls the stdlib `subprocess.Popen(...)` with `shell=True` (that is exactly why bandit needs the `# nosec B604` marker, and why the assertion message itself says "the shell=True popen( line"). `subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, ...)  # nosec B604` does **not** contain the substring `popen(` — the token is `Popen(` with an uppercase `P`. Concretely, for a source line such as

```python
    return subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE)  # nosec B604
```

`"shell=True" in ln` is true but `"popen(" in ln` is false, so the generator yields nothing and `next()` raises `StopIteration`. The test therefore errors out (or fails) even though the code under test is perfectly correct, instead of passing. The predicate needs to match the actual token, e.g. `"Popen(" in ln` (or `re.search(r"[Pp]open\(", ln)`), otherwise the regression test for B7c31db560d can never be satisfied.

chunk_findings.detail: The generator `next(ln for ln in src.splitlines() if "shell=True" in ln and "popen(" in ln)` filters on the lowercase substring `popen(`. The shell-spawning call it is supposed to inspect is a subprocess call: either `subprocess.Popen(cmd, shell=True, ...)` (capital `P`) or `subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, ...)`. The lowercase string `popen(` is a substring of neither — `Popen(` starts with an uppercase `P`, and `run(`/`call(` never contain `popen(` at all. With either standard implementation, the generator yields nothing and `next()` raises `StopIteration`, so the test errors out instead of performing its `assert "nosec B604" in call` check. The prior version of this test used the correctly-cased anchor `"P.run("`; switching to lower-case `popen(` means the only line that could satisfy the filter is a user-defined function literally named `popen`, which is not the subprocess API the marker is about (and a real `Popen(..., shell=True)` line would be bandit B602, not B604, so even the marker string would not match). The test therefore cannot validate the claim in its own docstring.
